lessons.title: Lesson 1: Know yourself before you choose
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write down your interests, strengths, learning style and money needs so you can judge each path.
This lesson builds toward: Before comparing schools or jobs, you will list your interests, strengths, learning style and money needs, and choose the paths that fit best so far, circling two or three of the five main paths.
Before you compare schools or jobs, look at yourself. The best path fits what you enjoy, what you are good at, how you like to learn, and what you need right now.
Ask yourself: What subjects or activities make time fly? Do I learn best by reading and writing, or by doing things with my hands? Do I need to earn money soon, to help my family or pay my own way? Do I want to stay close to home or move?
There are five main paths: a four-year college, a community college, a trade school or apprenticeship, the military, and going to work. None is better for everyone. A path that is great for a friend might not fit you.
An AI assistant can help you brainstorm careers that match your answers. Treat its ideas as a starting list, then check real facts with a counselor and official websites.
Step by step:
- Write three things you enjoy and three things you are good at.
- Write how you learn best: reading, listening or doing.
- Write your money needs: do you need to earn soon?
- Write where you want to live for the next two years.
- List the five paths and circle the two or three that fit best so far.
Words to know:
- Interest: something you enjoy doing or learning about.
- Strength: something you do well.
- Path: the route you take after school toward a career.
Try it now: Answer the four questions in this lesson on paper. Then ask an AI assistant: Here are my interests and strengths. Suggest five careers and the training each needs. Circle the two or three paths that fit you best.
You can now describe your interests, strengths, learning style and money needs, and pick the paths worth comparing.

check.q: What are the five main paths after high school in this course?
options: College, gap year, travel, sports and music
Four-year college, community college, trade school or apprenticeship, the military, and work
check.why: The course compares these five paths, and many people mix them over time.

check.q: You need to earn money soon to help your family. How does that affect your choice?
options: Look closely at paths where you can earn while you learn, like an apprenticeship or work with training
Only a four-year college is possible
Wait a few years before deciding
check.why: Your money needs are part of what makes a path fit you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Community college and four-year college
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare a community college and a four-year college using the same five questions.
This lesson builds toward: Using school websites and net price calculators, you will compare a community college and a four-year college using the same five questions, with every question answered or marked to ask.
A community college is a public, two-year college close to home. It offers certificates (often a year or less), associate degrees (about two years), and classes you can transfer to a four-year college. It usually costs much less and lets you live at home.
A four-year college or university offers bachelor's degrees. Some careers, such as teaching, nursing with a bachelor's degree, engineering and accounting, usually need one. Costs vary a lot between public and private schools and between living at home and in a dorm.
Use the same five questions for every option: What will it cost in total, after aid? How long will it take? Can I earn money while I learn? What jobs do graduates get, and what do they earn? What do I need to get in?
A smart route for many students is to start at community college and transfer. Ask the community college which four-year schools accept its credits before you sign up for classes.
Step by step:
- Pick one community college and one four-year college to compare.
- Look up each school's total yearly cost and its net price calculator.
- Write the time to finish, the jobs graduates get and what you need to get in.
- Ask a counselor about transfer agreements.
- Put the answers side by side in a table.
Words to know:
- Certificate: a short program that trains you for a specific job.
- Associate degree: a degree that usually takes about two years.
- Bachelor's degree: a degree that usually takes about four years.
- Transfer: moving your college credits to another school.
- Net price: what college costs after grants and scholarships are taken off.
Try it now: Make a table with the five questions down the side and two schools across the top: one community college and one four-year college. Fill in what you can find on their websites and mark what you still need to ask.
You can now compare a community college and a four-year college with the same five questions and spot a start-and-transfer route.

check.q: What does a net price calculator show?
options: An estimate of what a school costs after grants and scholarships
How many students live in dorms
check.why: Net price is what college costs after grants and scholarships.

check.q: You compare two colleges but only look at the sticker price. What are you missing?
options: Nothing; price is all that matters
The other questions: time, earning while learning, jobs and pay, and what you need to get in
check.why: Use the same five questions for every option.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Trades, apprenticeships, the military and work
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare an apprenticeship, the military and a job with training using the same five questions.
This lesson builds toward: Using apprenticeship.gov and official sources, you will compare an apprenticeship, the military or a job with training using the same five questions, asking about finish rates, job placement and accreditation before signing anything.
A Registered Apprenticeship is a job where you are paid while you learn a skilled trade or occupation from experienced workers, with classes on the side. Trades include electrician, plumber, carpenter and welder, and there are apprenticeships in health care, IT and more. Search the Apprenticeship Job Finder on apprenticeship.gov.
Trade schools teach a skill in months instead of years, but you usually pay. Before you sign, ask how many students finish, how many get jobs in the field, and whether the school is accredited. Be careful of high-pressure sales.
The military offers job training, pay, and education benefits, in exchange for a service commitment of several years. You take a test called the ASVAB, which helps decide which jobs you qualify for. Talk to recruiters from more than one branch, read everything before you sign, and check the branch's official website.
Going straight to work is a real path too. Look for employers that train you, promote from within, or help pay for classes later. Use the same five questions to compare these paths to college.
Step by step:
- Search apprenticeship.gov's Apprenticeship Job Finder for programs near you.
- For any trade school, ask about finish rates, job placement and accreditation.
- If you are thinking about the military, talk to more than one branch and read before signing.
- For jobs, look for training, promotion and tuition help.
- Answer the five questions for each option.
Words to know:
- Registered Apprenticeship: a paid job with structured training that leads to a recognized credential.
- Trade: a skilled job you learn by training, like electrician or welder.
- Accredited: checked and approved by an official group that reviews schools.
- ASVAB: the test used to see which military jobs you qualify for.
Official sources:
- Apprenticeship.gov: Apprenticeship Job Finder
- Apprenticeship.gov
Try it now: Find one apprenticeship near you on apprenticeship.gov and one job that offers training. Add them to your table from the last lesson and answer the five questions for each.
You can now compare apprenticeships, trade schools, the military and work with the same five questions you used for college.

check.q: What makes a Registered Apprenticeship different from a trade school?
options: You are paid while you learn on the job
check.why: In an apprenticeship you earn pay while learning from experienced workers.

check.q: A military recruiter wants you to sign today. What do you do?
options: Sign so you do not lose the spot
Ask a friend to sign for you
Talk to more than one branch, check the official website and read before signing
check.why: Read everything and compare branches before committing to several years of service.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Paying for it and planning

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The FAFSA and financial aid
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain the kinds of financial aid and get ready to fill out the FAFSA for free on studentaid.gov.
This lesson builds toward: Using studentaid.gov, you will explain the four kinds of financial aid and plan when and with whom you will file the FAFSA, with this year's opening date and deadlines written down and no fee paid.
Financial aid is money to help pay for college, community college and many trade schools. It comes in four kinds: grants and scholarships (you do not pay them back), work-study (a part-time job), and loans (you pay them back with interest).
The FAFSA (Free Application for Federal Student Aid) is the form that opens the door to federal aid, and many states and colleges use it for their own aid too. It is free and you fill it out at studentaid.gov. You will need a StudentAid.gov account, and so may a parent or other contributor whose information is on the form.
A new FAFSA opens each year for the next school year. Check studentaid.gov for the date it opens and check your state's and colleges' deadlines; some aid runs out early, so file as soon as you can.
Never pay anyone to fill out the FAFSA, and never share your StudentAid.gov username and password (your FSA ID) with anyone, including a consultant. Your school counselor or a college financial aid office can help you for free.
Step by step:
- Go to studentaid.gov (check the address carefully).
- Create your StudentAid.gov account; a parent or contributor may need one too.
- Gather what the form asks for, such as tax information.
- Look up this year's FAFSA opening date and your state and college deadlines.
- Fill it out early, or with a counselor's free help; never pay a company to do it.
Words to know:
- FAFSA: the Free Application for Federal Student Aid.
- Grant: money for school you do not pay back.
- Work-study: a part-time job that helps pay for school.
- Loan: borrowed money you must pay back, usually with interest.
- FSA ID: your StudentAid.gov username and password; never share it.
Official sources:
- Federal Student Aid: Apply for aid with the FAFSA
- FTC: How to avoid scholarship and financial aid scams
Try it now: Go to studentaid.gov and find this year's FAFSA opening date. Then find the financial aid deadline for one school and your state. Write both dates down, and write who will help you fill out the form.
You can now explain grants, scholarships, work-study and loans, and get ready to file the free FAFSA safely and on time.

check.q: Which kinds of aid do you not pay back?
check.why: Grants and scholarships are free money; loans are paid back with interest.

check.q: A website ending in .com offers to file your FAFSA for a fee. What do you do?
options: File for free at studentaid.gov or with a counselor's help
check.why: The FAFSA is free at studentaid.gov; never pay to file it or share your FSA ID.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Avoiding debt traps and scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare aid offers and spot the warning signs of debt traps and scams.
This lesson builds toward: Given aid offers and scholarship offers, you will sort each offer into free money, earned money and loans, calculate what is left to pay, and spot scam warning signs, getting the amounts right and naming where to report a scam.
Debt is not always bad, but too much can follow you for years. Borrow only what you need after grants and scholarships. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says to use federal student loans before private ones, because federal loans usually have more protections.
When you get aid offers, check each line: is it a grant, a scholarship, work-study or a loan? Some offers mix them together so loans look like free money. Compare the cost left over at each school, not just the size of the offer.
Scam warning signs, from the Federal Trade Commission: a scholarship that is guaranteed; a fee to apply or to hold a scholarship; asking for your bank or card number; telling you that you won a contest you never entered; and pressure to pay right now. Real scholarships do not charge you to apply.
Watch for schools that push you to sign up and borrow fast, promise jobs they cannot prove, or will not tell you their graduation and job numbers. If you are scammed, report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Sort each aid offer into grants, scholarships, work-study and loans.
- Work out what is left to pay at each school.
- Use federal loans before private loans, and borrow only what you need.
- Check every scholarship offer against the scam signs.
- Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Words to know:
- Interest: the extra money you pay for borrowing.
- Federal student loan: a loan from the US government with set protections.
- Private loan: a loan from a bank or company, often with fewer protections.
- Debt trap: debt that grows faster than you can pay it off.
Official sources:
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Student loans
- FTC: How to avoid scholarship and financial aid scams
Try it now: Look at this example offer: $3,000 grant, $2,000 scholarship, $2,500 work-study, $5,500 loan, for a school that costs $14,000 a year. Write how much is free money, how much must be earned or paid back, and how much is still left to pay. (Free: $5,000. Earned: $2,500. Loan: $5,500. Still left: $1,000.)
You can now read an aid offer line by line, borrow carefully, and spot financial aid scams and pushy schools.

check.q: Why read each line of an aid offer?
options: Some offers mix loans in so they look like free money
Aid offers are always all grants
check.why: Sorting grants, scholarships, work-study and loans shows what you will really pay.

check.q: An email says you won a scholarship you never applied for and asks for your bank number. What is it?
options: A scam warning sign; do not give your bank number
check.why: Contests you never entered and requests for bank numbers are scam signs.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making your two-year plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a two-year plan with a main path, a backup, money and milestones.
This lesson builds toward: Using your comparisons and aid plan, you will write a two-year plan with a main path, a backup, six-month milestones, how you will pay and who will help, with every part included and a date to review it.
A plan turns your choice into steps. Two years is long enough to make real progress and short enough to see clearly.
Choose a main path and a backup. For example: main path, an electrician apprenticeship; backup, a one-year certificate at community college while working. The backup keeps you moving if the main path is delayed.
Break the two years into six-month steps, with one or two milestones each: apply, take a test, finish a class, save a certain amount, get a first job in the field. Write how you will pay for each step and who will help you, such as a counselor, a parent, a coach, a mentor or a boss.
Look at your plan every few months. Plans change, and that is fine. Updating it is part of the skill.
Step by step:
- Write your main path and a backup.
- Copy in your five-question comparison for both.
- Split two years into four six-month steps, each with one or two milestones.
- Write how you will pay for each step.
- List the people who will help you.
- Set a date to review the plan every few months.
Words to know:
- Milestone: a clear step that shows progress, like finishing a class.
- Backup plan: a second path you can use if the first one is delayed.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page two-year plan with a main path and backup, your five-question comparison of at least two paths, how you will pay, your six-month milestones and the people who will help. Show it to a counselor or adult you trust.
You can now write a two-year plan with a main path, a backup, milestones, a way to pay and people to help, and update it as life changes.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Main path and backup Only one path, or the path does not connect to the learner's interests and needs. A main path and a backup that fit the learner's interests, strengths and money needs. Explains why the backup still moves them toward their goal. Five-question comparison Fewer than two paths compared, or questions skipped. At least two paths compared on cost, time, pay while learning, likely jobs and what you need to get in. Uses net price or apprenticeship pay from official sources and notes where each answer came from. How to pay No money plan, or relies on unknown loans. Says how each step will be paid for, including the FAFSA date and deadlines if aid is needed. Shows grants and scholarships first, loans last, and the amount left to pay. Safe from scams Plans to pay for FAFSA help or a guaranteed scholarship. No paid FAFSA help, no shared FSA ID, and no offers with scam signs. Names where to report a scam and who to ask for free help. Milestones and helpers No six-month steps or no helpers named. Four six-month steps with milestones, the people who will help, and a review date. Has been shown to a counselor or trusted adult, with their feedback noted. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a milestone in a two-year plan?
options: A clear step with a time, like finishing a class by June
check.why: Milestones break the plan into six-month steps you can check.

check.q: Your main path is delayed by six months. What does a good plan help you do?
options: Move to your backup path and keep making progress
check.why: A backup keeps you moving if the main path is delayed.
